first.rationale:
Two of the three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are directly observed regressions in our own funnel, whereas the competitor pricing threat is an external pressure that discounting would answer only by trading margin and likely attracting the least durable accounts. Given the objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, I intend to run the onboarding-shortening experiment (memory_86), which addresses the measured regression closest to the root of the funnel and plausibly propagates into the activation decline that memory_91 would address only downstream.

I am spending verification on memory_86 and memory_73 rather than on the memories I find most agreeable. memory_86 is the one I plan to act on, so its original record matters most: the consolidated summary reports direction ('improved completion', 'lifting early adoption') but no effect size, no durability window, and no segment breakdown. If the original showed a short-lived lift measured only at completion — a proxy metric that can move without any real gain in value delivered — the case weakens substantially. memory_31 is a closely related claim (signup simplification, day 12) and is the mechanism by which this direction could go wrong: cutting required fields can inflate activation counts while degrading lead quality and downstream qualified revenue, which is exactly the metric I am optimizing. I flag that risk explicitly and will instrument for it rather than spend a verification pull on it.

I verify memory_73 because it is the strongest competing option under current conditions and the one whose summary most conspicuously omits what I need. 'Strong acquisition and revenue lift' is silent on retention, margin, and cohort durability; promotional pricing is precisely the intervention that can look excellent on the metrics a growth summary retains while destroying long-term value. If the original record shows durable retained revenue, my ranking should change. If it shows only acquisition, I can set the pricing direction aside with justification instead of intuition.

Standing caveats: these are consolidated summaries, not primary records, and the oldest are 15-64 days stale in a market that has since shifted under competitive entry. All six memories describe wins, which suggests the archive may retain successes preferentially, so I treat the absence of recorded harm as weak evidence rather than evidence of safety. Prior effects were measured before the competitor launch and may not replicate. I therefore propose a standard experiment with a holdout, measuring not completion rate but downstream qualified revenue and 30-day retention per cohort, and I will revise if either verification contradicts the summary.

final.rationale:
Both verifications resolved in the direction that supports the intended action, and one of them resolved decisively against the main alternative.

exp_86 held up under inspection and held up on the metric that actually matters. The consolidated summary claimed only completion and adoption; the source adds 30-day retention +3% and time-to-value -2.1 days. That is the crucial addition, because my standing worry about onboarding work was that it moves a proxy (completion) without delivering real value. Positive retention alongside faster time-to-value is evidence the lift is substantive rather than cosmetic. Effect size is meaningful (+13%). I commit to simplify_onboarding.

exp_73 is the more valuable pull, because it inverted the inherited summary. memory_73 recorded 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' and dropped the fact that the acquired cohort loses 12% retention and does not survive first renewal — the original record explicitly warns against generalizing targeted discounting as sustainable growth. Under a mandate for sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional pricing is now ruled out, not merely deprioritized, despite being the intuitive response to the competitor's entry pricing. Note the general lesson: the consolidation step here preserved the favorable half of the finding and discarded the caveat. That raises my prior that other inherited summaries — memory_57's 'no measurable harm to retention', memory_31's 'durable lift' — are similarly optimistic compressions of records with warnings I cannot now check. I did not verify them and do not treat them as confirmed.

Residual uncertainty I am carrying rather than resolving: exp_86 ran on day 52 in a pre-competitor market, and its retention figure is 30-day, which is shorter than the renewal cycle that exposed exp_73's damage. A 30-day positive is reassuring but is not proof of durability past first renewal. Separately, memory_31 flags the live risk on this direction: stripping signup requirements can inflate activation while degrading lead quality, which would show up as weaker qualified revenue per account even as completion rises.

Execution accordingly: standard experiment with a randomized holdout, not a broad rollout, since prior conditions no longer obtain. Primary metric is qualified revenue per cohort, not completion. I will shorten and resequence the onboarding flow rather than delete qualification fields, so the tested change is the one exp_86 actually validated and not the adjacent unverified one. I will hold the cohort through first renewal before generalizing, applying exactly the standard that exp_73 failed. If qualified-revenue-per-account degrades while completion rises, that is a failure and I will report it as such rather than banking the proxy gain. The activation decline is left unaddressed this week; if onboarding improvement does not propagate into activation, activation_messaging is the next slot's candidate.
